prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock meets the test I apply to every file: it is an original invention, experimentally verified, and it opens a door. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first realisation made it possible to interrogate many atoms with the trap perturbation cancelled, and Ye's group took the same idea to the 10^-18 regime with systematic control that other laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) have since reproduced. The consequences are concrete: millimetre-scale relativistic geodesy, tighter tests of constant variation and dark-matter couplings, and the pending redefinition of the second. The credit is also unusually clean. Two named people, one proposer-and-first-realiser and one who brought it to record performance, fit the record without forcing us to choose among collaboration members. Four of eight opening ballots place it in the top three, the broadest support on the shortlist, and the support comes from different subfields.
statement.case_against: Frequency combs (2005) and ion-trap control (2012) have already been honoured, and a sceptic can read lattice clocks as an extension of recognised metrology rather than a new discovery; Goran Johansson's rank of seventh reflects this. Other lattice-clock groups (Yb at NIST, Hg and Sr in Paris, Sr at PTB) have comparable claims on specific milestones that I cannot settle from the supplied names. If the committee prefers to wait for the SI second redefinition, the case is delayed but not weakened. My own first-ranked candidate, aberration-corrected electron optics (B021), remains in my view the more transformative tool for materials physics, but I stand alone on it, I am a microscopist with an obvious bias, and the credit question around Knut Urban is unresolved. I do not think I can responsibly put it forward as the preferred prize while that historical record is unchecked.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as the clearest case of a new measurement technique opening new ways of observing nature, with a natural two-person prize, while noting that others (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow) sit outside the supplied credit and that the committee might wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree with the framing and the two names. I would answer the redefinition worry directly: the Nobel Prize rewards the demonstrated invention, not a metrology committee's timetable, and the 10^-18 performance has already been reproduced independently. I do ask that the committee check the archival record of who first demonstrated the magic-wavelength lattice, since Takamoto's role in the RIKEN realisation needs to be understood before we write the citation. I also note that Kroll's own interest in quantum memories (B007) makes his ranking of B007 second a declared conflict, and I would weight that entry accordingly.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B036 first because the magic-wavelength idea makes atomic structure and light-shift theory into an instrument with clear fundamental content, and she asks whether a prize should be shared with the ion-clock lineage or comb contributors already honoured.
responses.response: I share the view that this is atomic physics turned into an instrument. On the ion-clock question I would not widen the prize: Wineland's 2012 citation was for manipulating single quantum systems, and the lattice clock's distinguishing step is the use of many neutral atoms with the trap shift cancelled, which is a different invention. Widening it would push the count beyond two without improving the attribution. Her second-ranked B049 is a fine piece of theory, but strong-field recollision overlaps the 2023 attosecond prize, and she has rightly disclosed her closeness to a 2023 laureate.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a basic-physics demonstration that became the common architecture of superconducting quantum optics, but concedes that Wallraff cannot be represented by the credited trio and that it may sit close to the 2025 circuit prize; he places lattice clocks seventh as an incremental extension of honoured metrology.
responses.response: I take the circuit QED case seriously, since strong coupling of a single microwave photon to an artificial atom was a genuine first. But I cannot support a trio that leaves out the experimentalist who is central to the first strong-coupling demonstration, and our own rule is that we must be sure we have the people who did the original experiment. The 2025 prize is also so recent that a second circuit prize looks unwise. I disagree with calling lattice clocks incremental: a comb is a ruler, whereas the lattice clock is a different clock whose accuracy comes from the atom rather than the trap, and no earlier prize covered that. I also note that you and I are both at Chalmers, which I flag below, but I do not think it affects my view of B044.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks time-reversal-invariant topological insulators first and magic-angle graphene second, and wants B022 as a two-person theory-plus-experiment prize, noting that the first authors of the 2018 papers and earlier moire theorists complicate credit.
responses.response: I agree that B022 is a strong, original and widely reproduced discovery, and that is why I keep it as an alternative. On the three names I would keep Bistritzer, since the 2011 flat-band prediction is his as much as MacDonald's, and cutting him to get a cleaner pair would answer the wrong question. I would also not choose B054: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang's HgTe proposal is missing from the credited names, so the experimental half rests on a prediction made by people who cannot all be named, and you have said yourself that the credit cannot be settled from the list.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks IceCube first as the instrument-driven opening of a new observational window, while accepting that the source associations rest largely on IceCube alone and that credit among builders and analysts is unresolved.
responses.response: I share the instinct, since a new window is what excites me most, and I ranked B012 fifth. My reservation is that the committee must name individuals for a result produced by a collaboration of hundreds, and the strongest source associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) lack independent confirmation at high significance. By contrast, the lattice clock has been reproduced by several separate laboratories. I would hold B012 for a later year when KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD confirm a source.

uncertainties: Priority among lattice-clock groups, in particular the roles of Takamoto and the RIKEN team and of the JILA, NIST and SYRTE groups, needs to be checked against the archival record.
Whether the committee will treat lattice clocks as a new invention or as a continuation of the comb and ion-clock prizes.
For B021, whether Knut Urban belongs among the credited names alongside Rose, Haider and Krivanek, and the priority of TEM versus STEM correction.
Whether the committee is prepared to wait for the redefinition of the second, which would affect timing but not attribution.
statement.conflict_note: Possible connection to flag: since 2025 I am a Fellow of the University of Tokyo and have long-running exchanges with Japanese microscopy communities, and Hidetoshi Katori is at the University of Tokyo. I have no known collaboration with him and do not believe this requires recusal, but the committee should know. I am also a microscopist, so I am biased toward B021, and my Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson ranked B044 first. No other specific conflict is apparent from my profile.
